title: Smoke, Drums and Fire on the Hills
summary: Long ago, nobody could just pick up a phone. To send news far away, people lit fires on hilltops, beat drums that copied the sound of words, sent runners racing along mountain roads, and even let birds carry tiny letters home. Every one of these tricks was clever, but each one was slow, easy to stop, or able to say only a few simple things.

sections.heading: A World That Moved at the Speed of Feet
paragraphs: Try a little experiment in your head. Your cousin lives 500 kilometres (about 300 miles) away, and you have big news: a new baby brother has just been born. Today the news would reach your cousin in less time than it takes to sneeze. Now take away every phone, computer, radio and wire. What is left? You could walk there, which might take about two weeks. You could ride a good horse and swap it for fresh ones along the way, which might take three or four days. You could hand a letter to a ship's captain and hope the winds were kind. That was it. For almost all of human history, news could travel no faster than the fastest thing that could carry it.

This is the giant problem at the very start of our story. A message is a kind of invisible cargo. It has no weight, but before electricity it still had to ride on something real: a person's memory, a scrap of papyrus, a knot in a string, a bird's leg. If the carrier was slow, the news was slow. If the carrier got lost, sick, captured or eaten by a wolf, the news simply vanished.

That mattered enormously. Kings needed to know when an enemy army crossed the border. Merchants needed to know whether a ship full of spices had arrived or sunk. Families needed to know whether a traveller was alive. Often, by the time the news arrived, it was already too late to do anything about it. Battles were sometimes fought after a peace treaty had already been signed, simply because nobody had told the soldiers.

So people all over the world, in completely different places and times, came up with tricks to make messages move faster than a walking human. Some used light, which travels incredibly fast. Some used sound, which is quick over short distances. Some used relay teams, so no single runner or horse ever got tired. Some even borrowed the amazing homing sense of birds. None of these tricks is a telephone, but all of them were attempts to solve the same puzzle the telephone would finally crack: how do you get a message across a great distance, quickly, without carrying it there yourself?

sections.heading: Fires on the Mountaintops
paragraphs: Light is the fastest thing in the universe. It covers about 300,000 kilometres every second, which means a flash on one hilltop reaches your eyes on another hilltop practically instantly. Ancient people did not know that number, but they certainly knew that a big fire on a high place could be seen from very far away, especially at night. That simple fact gave us the oldest long-distance signal of all: the signal fire, or beacon.

One of the most famous beacon chains in history comes not from a history book but from a play. In 458 BCE, in the city of Athens, the playwright Aeschylus presented a set of three tragedies called the Oresteia, which won first prize at a great theatre festival. The first play, Agamemnon, opens with a tired watchman lying on the roof of a palace in the Greek city of Argos. For a whole year he has stared into the dark, waiting for one particular fire. When it finally blazes on the horizon, it means that the Greek army has captured the city of Troy, far across the sea.

Later in the play, Queen Clytemnestra explains how the news got there so fast. She describes a chain of bonfires leaping from mountaintop to mountaintop: from Mount Ida near Troy, across the sea to the island of Lemnos, on to the huge peak of Mount Athos, and onward over many more hills until the last fire is lit within sight of Argos. Each team of watchers saw the fire before them and lit their own, passing the flame along like a relay baton made of light.

It is an exciting scene, but remember: Agamemnon is a play, a work of imagination about a legendary war. It is not a news report, and nobody knows whether such a chain was ever really built for the Trojan War, or whether the Trojan War even happened the way the old stories say. What the play does tell us is something real about Aeschylus's own time: Greek audiences in the 400s BCE clearly understood the idea of passing a fire signal from hill to hill. The idea had to be familiar for the story to make sense.

There was one big weakness with a single fire. It could only say one thing. Fire lit means yes; no fire means no. A computer scientist today would call that one 'bit' of information, the smallest possible piece of a message. A fire could shout 'Troy has fallen!' but it could not add 'and the king is coming home on Tuesday with ten ships.'

Clever Greeks tried to fix this. In the 300s BCE, a writer on warfare named Aeneas Tacticus described a 'water telegraph'. Two teams on two hills each had an identical pot of water with a floating rod inside, and the rod was marked with a list of prepared messages, such as 'cavalry has arrived' or 'send grain'. At a first torch signal, both teams opened a tap at the bottom of their pots. When the right message reached the top of the pot, the sender raised a torch again, and both closed their taps. Because the water had drained for the same length of time, the floating rods sank to the same mark, and the receiver could read which message was meant. About two centuries later, the historian Polybius described this method and grumbled that it still fell far short of what an army really needed, because you could only send messages someone had written on the rod in advance. Polybius described a better scheme too: arranging the letters of the alphabet in a grid and using different numbers of torches to point to each letter, so that any word could be spelled out, slowly, one letter at a time.

Centuries later, the Byzantine Empire, whose capital was Constantinople (today's Istanbul), built a real and well-recorded beacon line. In the 800s CE, during wars with Arab armies, a chain of fire stations stretched about 720 kilometres (450 miles) from a mountain pass called the Cilician Gates, in what is now southern Turkey, all the way to the lighthouse of the emperor's Great Palace. Reports credit a scholar called Leo the Mathematician with a clever upgrade. At each end of the line stood an identical water clock. Each of the twelve hours had its own pre-agreed meaning, perhaps 'invasion' at one hour and 'battle' at another. The hour at which the first fire was lit told the emperor what had happened. Modern experiments suggest a signal could race down the whole line in about an hour, when a horse rider would have needed many days.

sections.heading: Smoke by Day, Flame by Night on the Great Wall
paragraphs: Now travel east to China, to one of the most famous structures on Earth. The Great Wall is not really a single wall. It is a whole collection of walls, forts and towers built and rebuilt over roughly 2,000 years by different Chinese dynasties to guard the northern frontier. Many of the walls you see in photographs today were built or rebuilt under the Ming dynasty, which ruled from 1368 to 1644.

Along and near the walls stood beacon towers, sometimes placed on hilltops a few kilometres apart so that each one could see its neighbours. Guards in these towers watched the empty grasslands and mountains to the north. If raiders appeared, the guards sent a warning: thick columns of smoke during the day, which could be seen against the sky, and blazing fires at night, which could be seen against the darkness. Flags and drums sometimes helped too.

Chinese commanders also found a way to make their signals say a little more than 'danger'. Accounts of Ming-era rules describe how the number of smoke columns or fires, sometimes along with gunshots or firecracker bangs, gave a rough idea of how many enemies were coming. One fire might warn of a small band, while several fires at once warned of a huge army in the thousands. The exact rules changed between periods and places, but the basic idea was a code: an agreed list of signals with agreed meanings. Every long-distance system in this story, right up to Morse code and the telephone network, depends on that same idea.

How fast was it? Historians describe Great Wall signals travelling hundreds of kilometres in a matter of hours, passing inland toward garrisons and even the capital. That was far quicker than any galloping messenger. But think about the weak spots. Heavy rain could stop a fire. Thick fog could hide smoke. A sleepy or careless guard could break the whole chain. And the signal could still only say a few simple things, like 'raiders, many' or 'raiders, few'. If the commander wanted to know which valley they were in, what weapons they carried, or where they were heading, he still had to wait for a rider.

sections.heading: Beacon Hill: England Watches for the Armada
paragraphs: Let us jump to the summer of 1588 and to the green hills of southern England. King Philip II of Spain had gathered an enormous fleet, the Armada, of roughly 130 ships. His plan was to sail up the English Channel, link up with a Spanish army waiting in the Netherlands, and invade England to overthrow Queen Elizabeth I.

The English knew something was coming, but not exactly when. So for months they had kept beacons ready along the coast and inland. A beacon in Tudor England was often an iron basket or a tall pile of wood, tar and brush on a high spot, guarded by local men who took turns watching. Their instructions were simple: if you see the enemy fleet, or if you see the next beacon burning, light yours.

On 19 July 1588, by the calendar England used at the time (29 July by the calendar we use today), lookouts spotted the Armada off the Lizard, the southernmost tip of Cornwall. The fires began. The warning raced eastward and inland, from hill to hill, across Devon and Dorset and along the high chalk ridges of Sussex, toward London. Local histories name some of the hills in the chain, such as Ditchling Beacon and Firle Beacon in Sussex. Nobody today knows exactly how many beacons were actually lit or precisely how long the message took, but the system was designed to beat any horse by a huge margin.

Each fire did more than send news. It was also an alarm clock for a whole region. When the local beacon flared, militia men knew to grab their weapons and gather at agreed meeting points, and coastal towns knew to prepare their defences. The Armada itself was battered by English ships and later wrecked by terrible storms as it sailed home around Scotland and Ireland, and the invasion never happened.

You can still see traces of this system today. Many hills across England are called Beacon Hill, a clue that a signal fire once stood there. In 1988, for the 400th anniversary, people lit 461 beacons and bonfires across England and Wales, starting at Kynance Cove in Cornwall. The chain of flames reached Berwick-upon-Tweed in the far north of England in about 18 minutes.

sections.heading: Drums That Speak
paragraphs: Fire and smoke speak to the eyes. Now let us listen with our ears, in West Africa, where people developed something much cleverer than a simple alarm: drums that could imitate speech itself.

To understand how, you need to know a secret about many West African languages, such as Yoruba in what is now Nigeria and Twi, spoken by the Akan people of what is now Ghana. They are tonal languages. In a tonal language, the pitch of your voice, whether a syllable is said high, middle or low, changes the meaning of a word. In English, if you say 'cat' in a high voice or a low voice, it is still a cat. In Yoruba, two words with exactly the same consonants and vowels can mean completely different things depending on their tones. Yoruba uses three main tones: high, mid and low.

That means the 'tune' of a sentence carries a lot of its meaning. And a drum can play a tune. The most famous talking drums, such as the Yoruba dùndún, are shaped like an hourglass, wide at both ends and narrow in the middle. A drumhead made of skin covers each end, and the two heads are connected by many leather cords running down the sides. The drummer tucks the drum under one arm and hits it with a curved stick. By squeezing the cords with the arm, the drummer tightens the drumheads and the note goes higher. Relaxing the arm loosens them and the note goes lower. A skilled player can even slide the pitch during a single beat, so the drum seems to swoop and wobble like a voice.

The drum cannot make vowels or consonants, but it can copy the pitch, rhythm and loudness of speech. For listeners who grew up with the language, that pattern can be enough to recognise words and phrases. Among the Asante, part of the Akan people, a pair of large drums called atumpan was used for important messages and for 'speaking' at royal ceremonies, reciting proverbs and the praises of rulers.

There was still a problem: lots of different words share the same tone pattern. Drummers solved this with extra words. An English missionary named John F. Carrington, who lived for many years in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo and learned to drum himself, explained this in his 1949 book The Talking Drums of Africa. Drummers did not just beat a short word. They wrapped it in a longer, fixed phrase that could only fit one meaning, a bit like saying 'the moon that looks down at the earth' instead of just 'moon'. The extra beats made the message longer, but much harder to misunderstand. In some communities, each person had their own 'drum name', so a drummer could call a particular person by beating their name, followed by the sender's name and then the message.

How far could a drum talk? Under good conditions, a big drum could be heard several kilometres away, often reported as around 6 to 8 kilometres (4 to 5 miles), especially in the still air of evening. Drummers in the next village could then pass the message on, so news could travel much farther than one drum could reach. Talking drums are still played today, at festivals, in ceremonies and in popular music, and they are one of the best examples in history of people turning the patterns of human speech into another kind of signal. That idea, turning speech into a signal that can travel, sits at the very heart of the telephone.

sections.heading: Runners and Riders
paragraphs: Signals like fire and drums are fast, but they can only carry simple or carefully coded messages. If a ruler wanted to send a detailed order, a long letter or a report full of numbers, someone had to carry it. The great empires of the ancient world discovered that the trick was not to find one superhuman messenger. The trick was teamwork: a relay.

In ancient Persia, the Achaemenid Empire of rulers like Cyrus the Great and Darius the Great stretched from what is now Turkey to the borders of India. To hold this huge empire together, the Persians used the Royal Road, running about 2,700 kilometres (1,700 miles) from the city of Sardis, in western Turkey, to Susa, one of the royal capitals in what is now Iran. Along it stood relay stations about a day's ride apart, with fresh horses, food and riders. The Greek historian Herodotus, writing around 440 BCE, counted 111 stations along this road. A royal message was handed from rider to rider, so it never had to wait for a tired horse. Estimates suggest it could cross the whole road in about nine days, while an ordinary traveller on foot would need roughly 90.

Herodotus was so impressed that he wrote a line praising these riders, saying that nothing stopped them from finishing their stage, not snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor darkness. More than 2,300 years later, a version of his words was carved on the front of a large post office building in New York City, where it is often thought of as an unofficial motto of American mail carriers.

On the other side of the world, the Inca Empire built an even more amazing network in the steep Andes mountains of South America. Its roads, called the Qhapaq Ñan, stretched about 40,000 kilometres (25,000 miles) through lands that are now parts of Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Colombia, climbing over passes, across deserts and over rope bridges hung above deep gorges. The Inca had no horses and no wheeled carts. So they used human legs, organised brilliantly.

The messengers were called chasqui (also spelled chaski). Small huts stood beside the road at short intervals; most Spanish chroniclers described them as about half a league apart, roughly 2.5 kilometres, though others gave different figures. Runners waited at each hut. When a chasqui approached, he blew a trumpet made from a conch shell, called a pututu, so the next runner could get ready. As they ran side by side for a few steps, the first runner repeated the spoken message until the second had it right, or handed over a quipu. A quipu (or khipu) was a bundle of coloured strings with knots in particular positions. It mainly recorded numbers, like how much a village owed in taxes or how many soldiers to send, and trained record-keepers, rather than the runners themselves, were the experts at reading them.

Because each runner only sprinted a short stage and then rested, the message never slowed down. Sources often say the chasqui system could carry a message around 240 kilometres (150 miles) in a day, and some estimates go even higher. One Spanish chronicler, Martín de Murúa, wrote that runners brought fish from the sea to the ruler in Cusco, high in the mountains, while it was still fresh. That is a report written by a chronicler after the Spanish conquest, so treat it with care, but it shows how impressive the system seemed to people who saw it.

And what about the most famous messenger story of all? You may have heard that after the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE, when the Athenians defeated a Persian army, a runner called Pheidippides dashed about 40 kilometres to Athens, cried out the news of victory, and collapsed dead. It is a wonderful story, and it inspired the marathon race at the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. But it is a legend. Herodotus, who wrote within living memory of the battle, tells a different story: that before the battle, Pheidippides, a professional runner, was sent from Athens to Sparta to ask for help, covering about 240 kilometres in roughly two days. The tale of the run from Marathon to Athens and the dramatic death only appears in writers who lived around 500 years or more after the battle, and it became truly famous through a poem by Robert Browning in 1879. So: the Sparta run comes from our oldest source, while the deadly dash to Athens is best thought of as a legend.

sections.heading: Messages on Wings
paragraphs: There was one more messenger in the ancient world that could beat any runner or horse over long distances, and it did not need roads at all: the pigeon.

Homing pigeons have an astonishing ability. If you take one far from its home loft and release it, it will usually fly straight back home, often across hundreds of kilometres of unfamiliar land. Scientists still study exactly how they do it; pigeons seem to use the position of the Sun, Earth's magnetic field and landmarks, and possibly smells and very low sounds as well. People noticed this talent thousands of years ago, and some evidence suggests messages were being carried by pigeons in ancient Egypt more than 3,000 years ago.

The method is simple, but it has a catch. You tie a tiny, light message to the bird's leg and let it go, and it flies home. That means pigeons only carry messages in one direction: toward their home loft. To send news from a distant city back to your capital, you first had to carry pigeons from the capital to that city, in cages on horseback or by ship, and keep them there until needed.

Even so, pigeon post was used for an extremely long time. Roman writers mention pigeons carrying messages during a siege at Mutina, in northern Italy, in 43 BCE. In the Middle East, pigeon post became highly organised; by the 1100s CE, rulers had set up regular pigeon services linking Baghdad with cities in Syria, with lofts and keepers along the routes. A good homing pigeon can average roughly 80 to 95 kilometres per hour (50 to 60 miles per hour) over long flights, far faster than a horse can keep up for hours on end.
Pigeons had their own weak spots, though: they could be shot down or caught by hawks, they could get lost in storms, they would only fly home, and they could carry only a very small load.

sections.heading: Why None of It Was Enough
paragraphs: Let us line up everything we have seen and give each system an honest report card.

Beacon fires and smoke signals were incredibly fast, because they used light. But they were blind in fog, rain and snow; smoke was useless at night and small fires were hard to see by day. They needed teams of watchers sitting on cold hilltops for weeks or months, waiting for something that might never happen. Worst of all, they could say very little: usually a yes-or-no warning, or a handful of codes agreed in advance. If something happened that nobody had planned a signal for, the beacons were silent.

Talking drums could send real phrases, but only to listeners who knew the language and the drum's special phrases, and only as far as the sound carried, often a few kilometres. Wind, rain and the noise of everyday life could drown them out.

Relay runners and riders could carry long, detailed messages and even objects, but they were limited by the speed of legs, hooves and roads. The best relay systems in history could move a message a few hundred kilometres in a day. That is amazing for a human team, but it meant news from a far corner of an empire could still be weeks old by the time it arrived. Rivers flooded, bridges collapsed, messengers fell ill or were captured.
Pigeons were quick, but they only flew one way, carried tiny loads and did not always arrive.

So by the 1700s, after thousands of years, humanity was stuck. Messages over long distances were either fast but simple, or detailed but slow. Nobody had found a way to send a detailed message quickly over a long distance, in any weather, by day or night. And absolutely nobody could send the sound of their actual voice farther than they could shout.

But the world was changing. The 1700s were the age of the Enlightenment, when scientists and inventors were measuring, testing and questioning everything. Telescopes were getting better, making it possible to see small details on a far-off hill. In France, a revolution was about to tear the old kingdom apart and leave the new government desperate for fast news from its armies at the borders. And in a small town in the French countryside, a young man and his brothers were wondering: what if, instead of one fire meaning one thing, you built towers with big moving arms that could spell out whole sentences? What if a message could fly faster than any runner, not by fire, but by shape? In the 1790s, Claude Chappe was about to find out.

deepDive: Historians of communication often describe all the systems in this part with two measurements that engineers still use today: speed (how quickly a signal crosses a distance) and capacity (how much information it can carry). Ancient methods were forced to trade one for the other. A beacon signal moved at the speed of light between stations, but the real delay came from people: a watcher had to notice the fire and then light their own, which takes minutes. Even so, a well-run chain could cross hundreds of kilometres in about an hour, as modern tests of the Byzantine line suggest. Its capacity, however, was tiny. A single fire carries one bit of information (yes or no). The Byzantine water-clock trick raised this to one of twelve messages, about 3.6 bits, by adding time as a second dimension. Aeneas Tacticus's water telegraph did something similar, using the time between torch signals to select one message from a prepared list. Polybius's alphabet grid was a conceptual leap, because it could in principle spell anything, but it was painfully slow. Relay couriers had the opposite profile: huge capacity (a whole letter, a quipu full of numbers, even goods) but low speed, a few hundred kilometres per day at most. Historians also debate how reliable some famous numbers are. Figures for chasqui speed come mainly from Spanish chroniclers writing after the conquest and from modern estimates, and they range from about 240 to over 300 kilometres per day, partly because sources disagree on how far apart the relay huts were. Herodotus's count of 111 stations on the Royal Road is respected but cannot be checked directly. Literary sources need special care: Aeschylus's beacon chain tells us what fifth-century Athenians found believable, not what happened at Troy, and the Marathon-to-Athens death run grew from much later writers such as Plutarch and Lucian before Robert Browning's 1879 poem fixed it in popular memory. Talking drums raise a different question that linguists find fascinating: they show that a language's tones alone can carry enough information to be understood, if extra 'redundant' phrases are added to remove ambiguity. Engineers would recognise this as an early example of error correction, the same principle that helps modern phones repair scrambled data.
funFact: When England lit 461 beacons in 1988 to mark the 400th anniversary of the Spanish Armada, the chain of fires ran from Cornwall to Berwick-upon-Tweed in about 18 minutes.
